Resources & FAQ

Common questions and myths, plain-language definitions, and links to official sources.

Frequently asked questions

Understanding your deadlines (read this one first)

This is the part people get tripped up on. There are two clocks running at once — your FAVN blood test and your rabies vaccine's protection period — and one is forgiving while the other is not. Here's the whole thing, broken down step by step with a worked example.

How does the FAVN blood test's timing actually work?

Two numbers matter, and both are counted from the date of the blood draw: 180 days and 2 years. The 180 days is a mandatory minimum wait — your dog can't enter Japan until at least 180 days have passed since the blood was drawn (a dog that arrives early is held in quarantine at the airport for the missing days), and there's no way to speed it up. The 2 years is the shelf life of that one test result, as long as your dog's rabies vaccine coverage stays continuous the whole time (more on that below). So with a single FAVN test, your usable travel window runs from 180 days after the draw through 2 years after the draw. Example: blood drawn January 1, 2026 → you could travel any time from about June 30, 2026 through January 1, 2028, using that same test, no retesting needed in between. The 180 days counts from a passing test: if a result comes back below 0.5 IU/mL, your dog needs a new test, and the wait runs from that new, passing draw.

What if my trip might happen after that 2-year window closes?

Get a second antibody test whose result covers your arrival date. You do NOT need another 180-day wait after it, as long as three conditions all hold: your dog's rabies vaccination has been continuous since the first dose, with no lapse; the second blood draw is at least 180 days after the first one; and the second titer is 0.5 IU/mL or higher. Once those hold, the second result counts as soon as it's back from the lab, and you have 2 years from the second draw to arrive. Worked example: first FAVN drawn January 1, 2026 → valid for arrival through January 1, 2028. If your trip moves to March 2028, get a second draw any time from about June 30, 2026 onward (leaving a few weeks for lab results before you need them), and it covers you for 2 years from that new draw — even if you only draw it after the first result has expired. The 180-day gap between draws is why a retest within the first 180 days doesn't qualify for this; there's rarely a reason to retest that early unless the first result failed. Japan doesn't require you to keep retesting every 2 years — only to have a valid result for your actual arrival.

So is there a deadline for that second antibody test?

Not a strict one — that's why it's the low-stakes clock. The only real constraint is practical: the result has to be back from the lab before you need it on your paperwork, so draw it a few weeks before your pre-export vet exam. Even if your first result has already expired, MAFF accepts a new test with no fresh 180-day wait, provided the rabies vaccination never lapsed. That's very different from the rabies booster below, where being a single day late resets everything.

What's the deadline on the rabies vaccine, and why is that buffer so much bigger (a month or more)?

This is the one to genuinely watch. Your dog's rabies vaccine has a labeled protection period printed on the vaccination certificate (commonly 1 or 3 years). As long as every booster is given before the previous one's protection period runs out, coverage counts as continuous — your FAVN result stays valid for its full 2-year life, and a later retest needs no new wait. But if that coverage lapses even briefly (a booster given even a day after the old one's protection technically ran out), Japan no longer accepts your existing FAVN result at all, regardless of how much of its 2-year window was left. This is the 'reset trap': you'd have to start completely over — a new vaccination series, a brand-new FAVN blood draw, and a fresh 180-day wait — six-plus months, from zero. That's why port.dog suggests a large safety buffer here (several weeks, scaled to your vaccine's labeled duration) — enough room that a delayed vet appointment doesn't turn into a six-month setback.

So what's the simple rule for how big a buffer should be?

Size the buffer to match the cost of being late. If missing a date just costs a short, predictable delay — like getting a second antibody test back from the lab — a small buffer is plenty. If missing a date resets the whole process and costs you months — a 'hard' failure, like a lapsed rabies booster — build in a much bigger buffer, and put an actual reminder on your calendar rather than trusting yourself to remember.

Paperwork myths & mix-ups

Does the FAVN report need to be signed in blue ink?

Not for Japan — but your own export authority may have its own rule. Japan's official guidance does not specify a signature ink color for the FAVN report or the health certificate; it prohibits pencil, erasable pen, and correction fluid/tape, but any pen color satisfies Japan. Your country's export authority can be stricter for its own endorsement appointment. CFIA in Canada, for example, requires a wet blue-ink vet signature on the rabies vaccination certificates you bring to the endorsement appointment, and recommends a wet-ink signature on the original Japan health certificate. Ask your export authority before the appointment rather than assuming either way.

Can I use my country's generic export health certificate instead of Form AC?

Only if it contains every item Japan requires — and generic templates usually don't. Japan accepts any certificate issued or endorsed by your government that covers all the required information, but strongly recommends its own Form AC so nothing is missed. Most countries' generic 'international health certificate' templates also say not to use them when the destination supplies its own form. The exception is a country that has negotiated a Japan-specific certificate (for example the UK's EHC 6407 or Spain's ASE-3293) — that one replaces Form AC. Check your country's note on the checklist.

Health & travel logistics

My dog has a heart condition (or is a flat-faced breed / senior / has mobility issues) — does that change the Japan paperwork?

Not the Japan import paperwork itself — but it absolutely matters for whether and how your dog should fly. Talk to your vet early about a fitness-to-fly assessment, and check your airline's own policies, since many restrict certain breeds or conditions from cargo or require extra documentation.

We have a brief layover or overnight stop in another country before Japan — does that need separate paperwork?

Possibly, yes. Even a same-day or overnight stop in a third country can trigger that country's own pet entry/transit rules, separate from anything Japan requires. Check directly with that country's relevant authority rather than assuming your Japan paperwork covers it.

At the airport

What actually happens at the airport if something's wrong with our paperwork?

Japan's Animal Quarantine Service reviews your documents on arrival. If everything was filed correctly in advance (including the 40-day notification) and matches up, this is usually quick. If something is missing, inconsistent, or a requirement wasn't met, your dog can be held in quarantine — potentially for as long as 180 days. Getting the paperwork right in advance is worth the effort.

Glossary

FAVN
Fluorescent Antibody Virus Neutralization test — the specific blood test Japan requires to measure your dog's rabies antibody level (titer) after vaccination. RFFIT is an accepted alternative test method.
Titer
The measured level of rabies antibodies in your dog's blood. Japan requires a result of 0.5 IU/mL or higher.
Designated laboratory
A laboratory Japan has specifically approved to run the FAVN/RFFIT test for import purposes — not every vet lab qualifies, so ask your vet which designated lab they use.
ISO microchip
A microchip meeting the ISO 11784/11785 standard, producing a 15-digit numeric code. Japan requires this exact standard, implanted before your dog's rabies vaccination series begins.
MAFF
Japan's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries — the government body that publishes the official animal import rules and runs the Animal Quarantine Service.
AQS
Animal Quarantine Service — the Japanese government office that reviews your paperwork, both in advance (the 40-day notification) and in person at the airport on arrival.
Form AC
Japan's recommended health certificate form for importing dogs and cats from non-designated regions, completed by your vet and endorsed by your government. Japan accepts another government certificate only if it contains every item Form AC covers. Designated regions use Form AB instead.
Designated region
A short list of countries/regions (currently including Iceland, Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Hawaii, and Guam) that Japan treats as rabies-free, allowing a simplified import process without a FAVN test. Most countries are NOT on this list.
Non-designated region
Any country not on Japan's designated (rabies-free) list — this covers the large majority of countries, including Canada, the US mainland, the UK, and most of the EU. This is the full FAVN-based process this app focuses on.
Government veterinary authority
Your country's official body that endorses export health certificates on behalf of the government — for example CFIA in Canada or APHIS in the United States. This is a separate, later step from your regular vet completing the paperwork.
